The two accent edges B–D and C–D form a smallest edge cut: removing both disconnects the graph and no single edge does. The card shows that cut and the edge connectivity 2." width="100%"} Returns the minimum number of edges whose removal disconnects the graph. For undirected graphs, this is computed as the minimum over strategic pairs of nodes. For directed graphs, respects edge directions. Edge connectivity provides a measure of graph robustness: higher values indicate more redundant paths and better fault tolerance. Time complexity: `O(V * E^2)` using max-flow computations. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Minimum number of edges needed to disconnect the graph. Returns `0` if already disconnected or has isolated nodes. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A cycle graph has two edge-disjoint paths between any pair of nodes (going each way around the cycle), so its edge connectivity is 2: ::: {#3528377a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() n = 6 for i in range(1, n + 1): graph.add_node(label=str(i)) for i in range(1, n + 1): graph.add_edge(str(i), str((i % n) + 1)) # Returns 2 graph.edge_connectivity() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: A star graph is much more fragile: removing the single edge to any leaf disconnects it from the rest of the graph: ::: {#8ab8f754 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_node(label="center") for i in range(1, 6): graph.add_node(label=str(i)) graph.add_edge("center", str(i)) # Returns 1 graph.edge_connectivity() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1 ``` ::: :::
